strengths: The paper tackles an original and important computer-vision/graphics problem: generating explicit, subject-specific internal muscle geometry from accessible surface motion observations. Connecting multi-view performance capture to layered anatomical animation could have substantial value for digital humans, sports, and medical visualization.

SKIM is a potentially valuable dataset contribution. The combination of five subjects, approximately 45 minutes of multi-view RGB, dense temporally consistent suit-marker trajectories, skeletal poses, static scans, layered anatomy, and marker-to-muscle associations is unusual and may enable future work beyond the proposed model.

The overall pipeline is coherent and technically motivated: canonical-space residual supervision separates non-rigid motion from skeletal articulation, while the coupled muscle/skin representation and smoothness, bending, stretching, tangential, and volume terms provide reasonable geometric priors for an otherwise severely underconstrained problem.

The evaluation considers several complementary properties rather than benchmark accuracy alone, including marker tracking, dynamic-region error, layer intersections, and volume preservation. The architectural and loss ablations show that the proposed priors substantially improve the volume metrics and that a nonlinear U-Net gives the best overall result.

The paper is clearly organized and visually polished. The problem formulation, capture pipeline, model components, and limitations are generally easy to follow, and the qualitative visualizations communicate the intended application effectively.
weaknesses: The central claim of recovering muscle deformation from real visual data is not convincingly validated. Training observations and tracking metrics concern only the outer suit/skin surface; the dynamic internal muscle geometry is inferred from a static fitted template and chosen regularizers. There is no dynamic MRI, ultrasound, biomechanical simulation, EMG, or other independent internal measurement showing that the predicted muscle shapes correspond to actual anatomy. The results therefore demonstrate one plausible regularized interior extrapolation, not recovery of true muscle deformation.

The method's internal predictions are fundamentally non-identifiable from the presented supervision. Many muscle fields could produce essentially the same exterior marker motion, and the proposed losses encode the desired answer rather than resolve this ambiguity empirically. Individual muscles are produced by propagating deformation from an aggregate boundary layer, but no per-muscle deformation, origin/insertion behavior, activation, or anatomical accuracy is quantitatively evaluated.

The baseline comparison is weak and partly mismatched. LBS is only a kinematic lower bound, while HIT is a static, generic-template tissue estimator rather than a subject-specific dynamic deformation method; its very large surface error is attributed to anatomical misalignment. Missing comparisons include subject-specific pose-space deformation models, marker-driven surface correctives coupled with alternative interior interpolation, and simulation-derived approaches. Several HIT entries are also unavailable, preventing a complete anatomical comparison.

The quantitative evidence does not fully support the paper's strongest wording. SOMA's mean marker error is slightly worse than LBS (13.43 versus 13.11 mm), its reported intersection ratios are nonzero despite the claim of strictly avoiding interpenetration, and deep muscle-to-bone volume deviation remains 10.35%. Moreover, volume preservation and collision metrics closely reflect quantities directly optimized by the proposed losses, so they are not independent evidence of biological correctness.

The experimental reporting is insufficient for judging robustness and reproducibility from the supplied manuscript. Important details such as per-subject results and variance, train/validation sequence construction, motion diversity, marker count and visibility, model architecture and parameter count, loss weights, training cost, inference speed, and sensitivity to tracking or template errors are absent or deferred to an unavailable supplement. With only five subjects and subject-specific training, evidence for consistent performance is limited.

The capture assumptions substantially narrow the contribution: each subject requires a 120-camera studio, a custom marker suit, a separate 140-camera scan, anatomical template fitting, and subject-specific model training. Thus the claim of a scalable and cost-effective vision-based solution is overstated, and inference from ordinary RGB imagery is not demonstrated; only skeletal pose is used at inference.

Possible measurement confounds are not analyzed. Stretching or sliding of the suit relative to skin, marker triangulation and pose-estimation errors, inverse blended-transform instability, and inaccuracies in the heuristic volumetric anatomy fit may all be absorbed as apparent soft-tissue deformation. The paper provides no uncertainty analysis or validation of marker-to-muscle associations.

No contribution type is explicitly declared, so I assess this as Algorithms/General while recognizing a strong dataset/proof-of-concept component. Under that standard, the originality is promising, but the lack of independent evidence for the principal internal-anatomy claim slightly outweighs the contribution. Framing the work more narrowly as concept-and-feasibility and validating against even limited internal ground truth would materially strengthen the case.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and underexplored problem: producing subject-specific, dynamically deforming internal anatomy from accessible surface-motion captures. The combination of the SKIM capture setup, a layered representation, and real-time animation could be useful for graphics and digital-human research.

The custom ArUco suit and large multi-camera setup provide temporally consistent, dense surface correspondences for five subjects and 45 minutes of motion. This is a meaningful data-acquisition effort, even though the resulting supervision is limited to the surface.

The formulation is clearly presented and incorporates reasonable geometric regularizers for smoothness, stretching, tangential motion, volume preservation, and interpenetration. The ablations show that these priors substantially reduce the model's own volume-deviation metrics. The figures also communicate the pipeline effectively. weaknesses: The central claim of recovering muscle deformation is not adequately validated. There is no dynamic in-vivo internal-anatomy ground truth: all data supervision comes from skin markers, while the internal motion is selected by hand-designed geometric priors and transferred from an approximate fitted template. Marker accuracy, volume preservation, and low self-intersection therefore do not demonstrate that the predicted muscles match real muscle motion, contraction, origins, or insertions. Describing the output as anatomically accurate or recovered from real data is substantially stronger than the evidence supports.

Despite the framing as inference from RGB or surface observations, the deployed model maps skeletal pose directly to deformation. It consequently cannot distinguish different muscle activations, loads, contacts, or exertion levels at the same pose. This fundamental non-identifiability is especially important for the proposed biomechanics, sports, and medical applications, but it is neither tested nor sufficiently reflected in the claims.

The quantitative comparison is weak and partially unfavorable. SOMA has worse mean marker error than simple LBS (13.43 versus 13.11 mm) and essentially identical intersection ratios. Its gains are confined to median, tail, and selected dynamic-region metrics. HIT is a generic, static, cross-topology model and consequently is not a well-matched dynamic, subject-specific baseline; its very large tracking error provides limited evidence for SOMA. Comparisons with simulation-derived deformation, captured muscle activations, or other subject-specific deformation models are absent.

The five-subject, subject-specific evaluation does not establish generalization beyond unseen poses of the same trained individuals. The manuscript omits important main-paper details such as per-subject results, variability or confidence intervals, demographics, motion coverage, exact train/validation splits, frame and marker counts, and sensitivity to marker noise or missing observations. It also does not test substantially out-of-distribution poses.

The physical metrics are closely aligned with quantities explicitly optimized by the proposed losses, making them weak independent evidence. Even under these metrics, deep-tissue volume changes remain 10.35%. The assertion that the method 'guarantees internal physical plausibility' is contradicted by nonzero intersections and by the lack of validation against actual internal anatomy or established biomechanical simulation.

Reproducibility is limited in the main manuscript: the U-Net organization for a pose-vector-to-mesh mapping, network dimensions, loss weights, optimization protocol, prism construction and filtering, individual-muscle binding, preprocessing, and baseline configurations are largely unspecified or deferred to unavailable supplementary material. The bibliography also contains a duplicate reference and several incomplete entries. Overall, the capture and animation prototype have merit, but consequential evidence gaps prevent the paper from substantiating its primary scientific claim.

strengths: The manuscript tackles an important and underexplored computer-vision problem: inferring dynamic internal anatomy from accessible surface observations. The combination of pose-conditioned deformation, explicit anatomical layers, and real captured motion is original and potentially useful for graphics, biomechanics, and digital-human applications. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/50427d4903344198a4cc2b5a247e8726/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

SKIM is a valuable systems/dataset contribution: it contains 45 minutes of multi-view recordings from five subjects, dense temporally tracked suit markers, skeletal poses, subject-specific scans, fitted anatomical templates, visibility masks, and residual deformation fields. The acquisition and correspondence pipeline is thoughtfully designed.

SOMA's coupled skin–muscle representation and biomechanically inspired regularizers provide a sensible way to resolve an otherwise severely underdetermined inverse problem. The volume, smoothness, stretching, bending, and sliding constraints are clearly motivated, and the ablations show that they substantially improve volume preservation.

Results on unseen motion sequences are encouraging. Relative to LBS, SOMA improves median and tail surface errors and reduces the reported dynamic-region error by more than half at the strictest threshold, while maintaining low intersection rates and much better subcutaneous-volume preservation.

The paper is well organized and visually clear, situates itself across vision, graphics, and biomechanics, acknowledges important limitations, and states that data and code are available. Although no contribution type is declared, the work is most compelling as a Datasets/Benchmarks plus Applied/Systems proof of feasibility rather than as a validated anatomical-reconstruction algorithm; judged in that framing, it makes a meaningful contribution.
weaknesses: The central claim of recovering muscle deformation is not directly validated. All dynamic observations lie on the skin, while the internal anatomy is initialized by surface-based template fitting and subsequently governed by hand-designed priors. Low marker error, volume change, and intersection rate demonstrate surface fidelity and geometric plausibility, but not that the inferred muscles match real in-vivo muscle shapes or activations. The wording should consistently distinguish plausible inferred anatomy from anatomically accurate recovery.

Evaluation is limited to unseen motions of the same five subjects using separate subject-specific models. There is no held-out-subject evaluation, and the manuscript does not report per-subject results, variability, dataset demographics, motion coverage, train/validation sizes, or uncertainty. This substantially limits conclusions about scalability and generalization.

The HIT comparison is difficult to interpret because HIT uses a generic SMPL-based topology whereas SOMA receives subject-specific scans, marker correspondences, and training sequences. The resulting 115 mm HIT error largely reflects anatomical/template mismatch. Stronger comparisons should include subject-specific pose-corrective surface models, alternative layered deformation methods, and matched-input baselines.

Several evaluation choices require stronger justification. The internal volume and intersection metrics are closely aligned with losses optimized by SOMA; deep muscle volume still changes by 10.35%; and the reported intersection rate is nearly identical to LBS despite claims that SOMA uniquely avoids interpenetration. External validation using dynamic MRI or ultrasound on selected muscles, EMG correlations, expert assessment, or comparisons with subject-specific simulations would considerably strengthen the case.

Reproducibility details are deferred too heavily to supplementary material: marker counts and coverage, tracking accuracy, network dimensions, optimization settings, loss weights, runtime, parameter count, split construction, and exact DRE aggregation are absent from the main paper. The assertion of real-time interactive use is also unsupported by measured speed.

Some claims are overstated. Inference is driven by skeletal pose rather than RGB directly, individual muscle meshes inherit deformation from an aggregate boundary rather than being independently reconstructed, and “arbitrary motion” is only tested on held-out sequences within captured subjects. Medical applicability should therefore be presented cautiously, and ethical/privacy considerations for releasing identifiable body scans would be appropriate.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored computer-vision problem: connecting observable surface motion to explicit, subject-specific internal anatomy. The combination of dense multi-view capture, layered templates, and real-time anatomical animation is original and potentially useful for graphics, sports, and biomechanical applications.

SKIM is a substantial acquisition effort: five subjects, approximately 225 minutes of synchronized 120-camera footage, dense ArUco tracking, skeletal poses, static skin/anatomy templates, visibility masks, and approximately 266K reconstructed 3D frames. The supplement provides useful details on subjects, exercises, marker processing, data organization, and coverage.

SOMA has a coherent formulation that separates muscle-boundary displacement from a skin residual and introduces smoothness, bending, stretching, tangential, and volume priors. The formulation is technically understandable, and the regularization ablations show that the physical terms substantially improve volume preservation.

Evaluation covers complementary surface and geometric measures rather than relying on average marker error alone. In particular, the dynamic-region, volume-change, and intersection metrics reveal deficiencies that global surface error can obscure. Results improve median and tail tracking errors over LBS while reducing subcutaneous volume error from 18.81% to 1.37%.

The paper is generally clear and visually polished, includes extensive supplementary material, acknowledges important limitations such as subject specificity and the absence of force/co-contraction conditioning, and states that data and code will be available.
weaknesses: The central claim of recovering muscle deformation is not convincingly validated. All dynamic supervision comes from external suit markers; no dynamic MRI, ultrasound, EMG, force measurement, or trusted simulation provides internal-muscle ground truth. Volume preservation and non-intersection are properties imposed by the method's own priors, not evidence that the inferred internal deformation matches real anatomy. Many internal solutions can explain the same skin motion, so the results establish a plausible animation prior more clearly than anatomical recovery.

At inference, the reported model is driven only by skeletal pose, not by RGB or observed skin deformation. Consequently it cannot distinguish different loads, contractions, fatigue, or co-contraction at the same pose. This conflicts with repeated framing such as recovery "directly from multi-view RGB data" and active-muscle inference, especially because weighted exercise is a major motivation of SKIM.

The supposedly individualized muscles are not learned or validated independently. A single deformation field on an aggregate muscle boundary is transferred to every high-resolution muscle through nearest-triangle barycentric binding. This does not model distinct origins, insertions, fiber directions, activation states, or relative sliding, and can cause nearby muscles to inherit essentially the same boundary motion. Figure 5 is qualitative and does not verify actual biceps geometry.

The empirical comparison is too limited for the claims. LBS is a weak kinematic baseline, while HIT is disadvantaged by generic SMPL anatomy and cross-topology mismatch, producing an extreme 115.34 mm mean error. Relevant learned soft-tissue/body-deformation approaches and simulation-based anatomical models are discussed but not evaluated. SOMA also has slightly worse mean marker error than LBS (13.43 versus 13.11 mm), and no uncertainty, per-subject results, statistical tests, or runtime/model-size measurements are reported.

Generalization evidence is narrow: the model is trained separately for each of only five subjects and tested on unspecified unseen sequences from those same subjects. The train/validation partition, sequence leakage prevention, frame counts per split, and whether hyperparameters were selected on the validation motions are not documented. There is no cross-subject, held-out-subject, cross-load, or same-pose/different-load experiment.

The architectural description is questionable. The supplement describes a flattened 207-D pose input followed by fully connected encoder/decoder layers and a direct 3N output, yet the paper calls this a U-Net and attributes its gain to "spatial weight-sharing." No mesh or spatial operation is specified, and the small advantage over the MLP is not sufficient to support that explanation.

Several reporting inconsistencies reduce confidence and reproducibility. The supplement claims over 330K unique time steps, whereas its dataset table totals 266K 3D-detected frames. It also refers to ground-truth "simulations" and vertex-to-vertex alignment although training is described as sparse marker supervision. Important choices such as the valid prism subset, anatomical fitting accuracy, marker/suit slippage error, mocap pose accuracy, and detailed data splits are not quantified.

Because the dataset contains identifiable multi-view recordings and detailed body scans, the submission should document participant consent, ethics approval or exemption, anonymization, permitted uses, and the release license. These governance details are absent. Overall, under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the capture system and plausible-animation method are promising, but the evidence does not yet substantiate the stronger anatomical-recovery claims. A Datasets/Benchmarks framing would still require clearer data validation, protocols, and ethics documentation.

strengths: The paper targets an important and difficult problem: augmenting surface-only digital humans with representations of internal soft tissue. The combination of capture, anatomical templates, learned pose correctives, and real-time visualization is potentially useful for graphics and vision applications.

SKIM represents a substantial acquisition effort: five subjects, approximately 225 total minutes at 25 Hz, a 120-camera setup, dense ArUco tracking, skeletal poses, and subject-specific skin, bone, and muscle templates. Providing raw and processed annotations could benefit future research on dynamic surface deformation.

The canonical residual formulation is sensible for separating non-rigid deformation from global articulation. The dual-layer model and its smoothness, bending, stretching, tangential, and volume regularizers form a coherent engineering pipeline.
The manuscript is generally clear and includes architecture and loss ablations, dynamic-region metrics, marker-visibility statistics, and qualitative visualization of multiple exercises.
weaknesses: The central claim of recovering muscle deformation is not validated. All dynamic supervision comes from markers on the external suit; the internal anatomy is a static template inferred from the outer scan using prior work. There is no dynamic MRI, ultrasound, instrumented, or simulation-based internal ground truth. Consequently, the experiments establish surface tracking and conformity to imposed priors, but cannot show that the inferred internal deformations correspond to real muscle behavior.

The surface-to-muscle decomposition is fundamentally non-identifiable from the supplied observations. Smoothness and volume penalties choose one plausible solution but do not make it anatomically correct. The reported volume-preservation and intersection metrics are also quantities directly optimized by the method, rather than independent evidence of anatomical fidelity.

The claimed individual-muscle modeling is especially weak. Individual meshes do not receive muscle-specific predictions; every vertex simply inherits the displacement of the nearest triangle on a unified inner boundary through barycentric transfer. The formulation includes no fiber directions, origins and insertions, activation, contraction, forces, or co-contraction. The paper itself acknowledges that behavior at fixed joint pose is unmodeled, even though such behavior is essential to distinguishing muscle dynamics from pose-conditioned geometric deformation.

The numerical evidence is not compelling. LBS has a slightly better global mean marker error than SOMA (13.11 versus 13.43 mm), and SOMA has exactly the same reported intersection ratios as LBS. Deep-tissue volume deviation remains 10.35%. Statements that the method guarantees plausibility or strictly avoids interpenetration are stronger than the nonzero errors support.

The baseline study is inadequate. HIT uses a generic SMPL-based topology and is explicitly disadvantaged by missing subject-specific proportions, making its 115.34 mm tracking error difficult to interpret. There is no competitive pose-dependent soft-tissue model, muscle simulation surrogate, subject-specific surface-corrective baseline, or equally supervised alternative that would isolate the benefit of the proposed internal decomposition. Architecture ablations provide only modest differences.

Generalization is very limited: the system is person-specific, uses only five subjects, and appears to test unseen sequences or poses within the same subjects. The manuscript does not clearly specify the train/validation split, possible temporal or motion overlap, per-subject results, variability, or statistical uncertainty. Thus it does not demonstrate generalization to new people or reliably new motion distributions.

The framing overstates the vision component. Multi-view RGB and the marker suit are used to construct training labels, but the learned model takes skeletal pose as input at inference; it does not recover muscles directly from arbitrary RGB observations. Moreover, suit stretch and slippage could differ from actual skin motion, yet no tracking-error, slippage, calibration, or repeatability validation is reported.

Several reproducibility and technical details remain unclear. The described 'U-Net' consumes a flattened pose vector and emits all vertex displacements, while the supplement lists fully connected dimensions but does not explain the claimed spatial weight sharing. The stability of inverting the blended rotation in the canonical-residual computation is not analyzed. Human-subject consent, data governance, and release/licensing conditions are also not documented in the manuscript.

No contribution type is declared, so I assessed the submission as Algorithms/General. Even if treated primarily as Datasets/Benchmarks, the main concern remains: SKIM contains rich external motion observations and fitted static anatomy, but no observed dynamic internal anatomy or benchmark protocol that could validate the task named in the paper. The work therefore has meaningful engineering and dataset merits, but consequential evidence gaps prevent acceptance.

strengths: The paper tackles an original and important computer-vision/graphics problem: connecting accessible multi-view surface observations to explicit internal anatomical animation. The combination of dense surface capture, subject-specific templates, and real-time muscle visualization has clear potential for digital-human applications.

SKIM is a substantial capture effort: five subjects, approximately 45 minutes per subject, 120-camera recordings, dense ArUco correspondences, skeletal poses, and layered meshes. The controlled resistance exercises are well chosen to expose pose-dependent soft-tissue motion. The paper is therefore best viewed as a hybrid Algorithms/General and Datasets/Benchmarks contribution; the dataset component materially strengthens its significance.

The layered formulation is technically coherent. Separating muscle and skin displacement fields and imposing smoothness, bending, stretching, tangential-motion, intersection, and prism-volume constraints is a sensible way to regularize an otherwise ill-posed problem.

The evaluation includes unseen-motion testing, dynamic-region errors, volume and intersection metrics, architecture comparisons, and loss ablations. SOMA notably improves median, tail, and dynamic-region marker errors over LBS, while reducing the reported subcutaneous-volume deviation to 1.37%.

The manuscript is generally clear and visually effective, provides equations and training hyperparameters, discusses meaningful limitations, and describes the dataset organization and preprocessing in useful detail.
weaknesses: The central anatomical claim is not adequately validated. SKIM observes skin markers, not dynamic muscles; its internal anatomy is initialized through template fitting rather than medical imaging, and no dynamic MRI, ultrasound, EMG, or simulation ground truth evaluates the inferred muscle deformations. Consequently, the experiments establish surface tracking and satisfaction of chosen priors, but not that the recovered internal motion is anatomically correct.

The decomposition is fundamentally non-identifiable: marker supervision constrains only the sum of muscle and skin-residual displacement, while the allocation between layers is selected by hand-designed regularizers. The individual muscles are subsequently deformed by transferring the aggregate boundary displacement, rather than being independently inferred or constrained by origins, insertions, fiber directions, activations, or muscle-specific mechanics. Calling these results recovered muscle behavior is therefore stronger than the evidence supports.

The model is pose-only and subject-specific at inference. It cannot represent load, force, fatigue, or co-contraction differences at the same pose—even though the dataset deliberately includes different resistance loads. Thus it primarily learns pose-correlated surface deformation and may average away precisely the activation effects that motivate the work.

The quantitative case is mixed. SOMA's mean global marker error (13.43 mm) is slightly worse than LBS (13.11 mm), its intersection ratios are essentially identical to LBS, and deep-tissue volume deviation remains 10.35%. HIT is a weakly matched comparator because it uses a generic SMPL-based topology and proportions, producing a 115.34 mm error; stronger subject-specific deformation, simulation, or graphics baselines are needed.

Experimental protocol and reproducibility details remain insufficient for judging generalization. The paper does not clearly specify the sequence-level train/validation split, variation across subjects or random seeds, per-subject results, uncertainty, or whether hyperparameters were selected on the reported validation motions. There is no held-out-subject evaluation, and only five subjects cover limited demographic and body-shape diversity.

Some presentation and dataset-accounting issues need correction: the described fully connected encoder-decoder does not substantiate the claimed U-Net spatial weight sharing; the reported 266K detected 3D frames is not reconciled with the claim of over 330K unique time steps; and privacy, consent, and release conditions for identifiable multi-view recordings and body scans should be stated.
